author: Ivan Shmalenko
headline: Co-founder at übernatural · Premium websites in 72 hours
title: Investors opening your site after the deck
text:
Investors opening your website right after a great pitch deck:

Most founders we work with sell on calls, in demos and in investor meetings.

So the website is the thing people open the moment the call ends.

Based on how your website represents you, people think about your company in specific ways. You can build something genuinely new and still look like someone reselling Chinese stuff.

When founders bring us a vibe-coded site, they very rarely defend it. Usually the first word they use is slop.

We've built 124 sites in Figma, Framer and Spline, including for government ministries. Our clients have raised $32M on them.

If you're raising and your site doesn't match the deck, happy to chat.

author: Ivan Shmalenko
headline: Co-founder at übernatural · Premium websites in 72 hours
title: Asking AI to change one headline
text:
Asking AI to change one headline on your homepage:

I use AI every day and I love it. But this happens quite often.

You ask Claude to change one thing on the homepage, and it changes pieces on pages you never mentioned.

Nobody notices until the numbers drop.

A human team understands the scope of what you asked. And when something goes wrong, you know exactly who is responsible.

author: Ivan Shmalenko
headline: Co-founder at übernatural · Premium websites in 72 hours
title: What 'AI built this' videos leave out
text:
Hundreds of accounts post websites with one caption: Claude built this.

A few of those sites were designed and built by my team.

We use AI on client work every day, so here are the parts those videos leave out.

The failed attempts. One usable image usually takes four or five prompt tries.

The designer upstream. Many prompt sites sell prompts that were built from real designs. I sell my designs to a couple of them myself, paid and credited.

The defects. AI B-roll can put you in a different room between two cuts. Claude misses it, while anyone with some video production experience sees it.

Two checks before you believe a demo. Is there a screen recording of the whole process, start to finish? And whose design went in before the prompt?

A real site like the ones in those videos is much closer to $30,000 to $50,000 per project.

author: Ivan Shmalenko
headline: Co-founder at übernatural · Premium websites in 72 hours
title: A $2,000 editor beats Claude's tokens
text:
A decent video editor costs about $2,000 a month. In my tests, that's cheaper than Claude's tokens.

I kept seeing videos that said AI edited this from start to finish.

So I installed everything I needed and tried it myself. Without a ton of correction, it just doesn't work. It doesn't do what you want it to do.

The one place it helped was B-roll for a launch video we're making. Claude generated it in the background while I worked on other stuff.

I could use around 20% of it.

The rest had defects Claude did not see. The shot was clearly in a very different room, sometimes with a different person. Anyone with some video production experience sees that instantly.

Deciding what belongs in the frame is still a human job.

That's how we use AI on client sites too. A designer does the base design in Figma and Framer, and AI generates only the specific assets that design calls for.

author: Ivan Shmalenko
headline: Co-founder at übernatural · Premium websites in 72 hours
title: Lovable went from $100M to $600M a year
text:
A million new projects a week are now built on Lovable, the app builder you prompt.

Its annualized revenue passed $600M in September, up from about $250M at the end of last year. Two thirds of the Fortune 500 have users on it.

I think for launching fast, this is probably the best thing a founder can do. Launching fast is always the most important thing.

What I watch is the other side.

Anything AI builds fully on its own has a fingerprint. Claude Design got better, but it overuses a specific set of elements, and anyone who has seen a lot of those sites spots it.

The moment a buyer spots it, the product feels less valuable.

My read, and it is pattern recognition, not a measured fact: a million projects a week means a lot more sites that look like each other. That makes looking different more expensive, and worth more.

Founders, when you land on a website, what's the first thing that tells you it came from a prompt?

author: Ivan Shmalenko
headline: Co-founder at übernatural · Premium websites in 72 hours
title: Higgsfield: $5.4B, and everyone has it
text:
Higgsfield is now worth $5.4 billion. It raised $400M in August.

Its annualized revenue hit $700M, up from about $200M at the end of last year. More than 30 million people use it, and 390 of the Fortune 500.

So everyone has access to the same tool now.

My team uses it too. For a villa that isn't built yet, we generated every asset in Higgsfield in about half a day. 3D modelling would have taken several weeks.

But one usable image still takes four or five prompt tries and 20 to 30 generations. Then an upscaler and Photoshop to remove the AI artifacts, before a designer places it on the page.

Image and video generation is extremely overpowered if you have taste. If you understand 3D, how to shoot and edit video, how to draw.

Without that, 30 million people just get the same slop faster.

The tool is the same for everyone. The eye that picks one image out of 30 is not.

author: Ivan Shmalenko
headline: Co-founder at übernatural · Premium websites in 72 hours
title: AI keeps moving the goalpost
text:
AI keeps moving the goalpost for web design.

Something you could have sold four or five years ago is basically unsellable now, because AI can make it quite simply.

The same tools work in the other direction too.

Things that used to need a big agency with lots of different talent, a small experienced team can create now. We're 13 people. We've shipped 124 sites for funded startups, $500M+ companies and government ministries, and our clients have raised $32M on them.

Our stack: Figma for design, Framer for the build, Spline for 3D and animation, and Claude, Higgsfield and Midjourney for the assets a design calls for.

What we make now is tenfold better than a year ago. Firstly, because our team became much, much better. Secondly, because the tools became better, so the same talent produces even crazier outcomes.

And unless a client is a designer themselves, they cannot reliably produce a site like that on their own.

So if you're judging your site against what looked premium two years ago, you're using a bar that has already moved. Happy to chat if you want a second pair of eyes on yours.

author: Ivan Shmalenko
headline: Co-founder at übernatural · Premium websites in 72 hours
title: Your homepage has 50 milliseconds
text:
People judge a website in about 50 milliseconds.

That's the classic Lindgaard study, and Google's own research measured first impressions forming in 17 to 50 milliseconds.

My design account on Instagram passed 30 million views in two years. Every video there is just my team's design work.

Two years of that left me with one rule. The design should be interactive, things should be moving, it should feel immersive.

The same rule decides a website hero.

One caveat I always give. If you sell to cold traffic from ads, load speed matters most, and animation should never stand between a buyer and the checkout.

Most of our clients sell through calls and demos. For a warm prospect, the first second is where your company starts to feel premium.

author: Ivan Shmalenko
headline: Co-founder at übernatural · Premium websites in 72 hours
title: How should an AI startup stand out?
text:
How should an AI startup stand out visually right now?

Most AI startups take their visual cues from other AI startups. Nature landscapes started as a way to look different from the old techie blueprint look. Now they're the new generic.

So stop looking at competitors. Go back to the roots of your industry: its history, the era when it was doing its best, the idea underneath the product.

Building for finance? Look at 1920s America. Space? The visual language of the 1960s. A product built on a concept like ontology? Dig into what that concept means and what it connects to.

Second point: the one-look test. If people can't recreate your brand in their head after seeing it once, it's bad branding. It skims past like a grey area.

We bring clients three to five directions built from those roots. Around 70 to 80% of the time they pick the one we were rooting for.

P.S. Or explore hiring us. Our clients raised $32M on sites we built.

author: Egor Galiy
headline: Team Lead Designer at übernatural · 400+ websites, 3 Awwwards
title: The Claude Design fingerprint
text:
Every site Claude Design makes carries the same tell.
I remove it on every project we ship.

One huge headline next to tiny uppercase text. Thin outlines around everything.

Once you've seen one site made by it, you've seen them all.

The fix is one instruction: drop the uppercase, change the composition.

Someone less experienced doesn't even know it's a cliche, because they haven't built up that much visual literacy yet.

So if your homepage has the giant font and the tiny caps, now you know where it came from.

author: Egor Galiy
headline: Team Lead Designer at übernatural · 400+ websites, 3 Awwwards
title: When Claude does the opposite of the prompt
text:
Some weeks Claude does the exact opposite of my prompt.
So I move the whole project to Cursor.

There's no clever signal behind the switch. It's a gut feeling, when there's a really obvious failure to do the task.

I hand the other tool a summary of the repo and carry on. When Codex starts working badly, I switch back to Claude.

Honestly, I have a feeling they slightly dumb down the models once they have a base of people who won't leave.

So the only loyalty I have is to the deadline.

author: Egor Galiy
headline: Team Lead Designer at übernatural · 400+ websites, 3 Awwwards
title: The 3D site with zero 3D in it
text:
A 3D forest on a website: three images, about 40 lines of code.
No 3D editor was opened.

When a client asks for a 3D site, most likely they just want a cool effect.

For me design is engineering. You pick the technology that gets the effect at the lowest cost.

So by default we fake it: generate the scene as a photo, animate it, tie it to the scroll or the mouse. A video puts less load on the visitor's processor and memory than a model.

For the forest, one photo plus a depth map and a normal map is enough, and the branches actually move under the mouse. Still a studio experiment, not client work yet.

Real 3D models are a luxury. We build them when there's a real need, a real budget and room in the timeline.

author: Egor Galiy
headline: Team Lead Designer at übernatural · 400+ websites, 3 Awwwards
title: The AI said 240 hours. It was 20.
text:
I asked an AI how much time our meeting bot saves us.
It said 240 hours a month. The real number is about 20.

Some context. I lead the design team at übernatural, a studio that sells websites to funded startups and ships each one in about 72 hours. There are 12 of us, and a lot of the work happens on short daily calls.

The AI assumed each of the 12 people sits in 2 to 4 calls a day. In reality it's 2 to 4 calls a day for the whole team.

The bot itself is simple. Read AI records every daily meeting, Claude splits the transcript into tasks, and one Telegram button drops the checklist into the right Notion project.

About 250 meetings a month, around $0.02 each, just under $7 a month all-in.

Before, someone had to rewatch a call at 2x speed and write the tasks down by hand.

The part I care about is the energy. We took one whole process out of a person's life, and now the document just lands in their hands.

And I check every flattering number an AI gives me, including the ones about our own work.

author: Egor Galiy
headline: Team Lead Designer at übernatural · 400+ websites, 3 Awwwards
title: Three kinds of designers
text:
There are three kinds of designers right now.
People who design, people who vibe-code, and people who do both.

The first group can design but doesn't build with AI. The second can prompt a whole site into existence but has never learned design. The third does both.

Before AI, there was only the first group, ranked by how good the design was. We sat somewhere in the middle. Plenty of studios were above us.

Then the models arrived and reshuffled the ranking. Not everyone who used to rank above us started using them. We did, and we try to keep up with every model that matters. So now we sit near the top.

The second group is the new one, and you can tell right away when a person has never touched design: composition problems, a style that drifts, the same overused templates I see every day.

A model can draw a decent-looking page now. I still point out its mistakes to it several times per page.

If you can't design, you don't see those mistakes, so you ship them.

Only the third group gets both halves: the model builds, a designer catches what it got wrong.

author: Egor Galiy
headline: Team Lead Designer at übernatural · 400+ websites, 3 Awwwards
title: The AI lead form that brings no better leads
text:
We built a lead form where AI asks you a follow-up question by name.
It doesn't get us better leads.

You can describe your company by voice instead of typing for five minutes.

After you submit, Claude reads what you wrote and asks one follow-up question, addressed to you by name, to dig into what you actually need.

I built it in half a day. We tested it for a week before it went live.

Stack: a regular form, Claude, Vercel, and an iFrame into Framer.

I'll be straight about it. It's more of a wow effect than a necessity.

It shows a founder, in the first minute, that we know how to build this kind of thing. I think that wow effect helps us sell websites. That's the main point of it.

We tried the idea once before, as a chatbot clients could add to their own landing page. Visitors barely touched it. Honestly, an unnecessary thing on a landing page.

If you'd like a form like ours on your own site, happy to chat about it.

author: Egor Galiy
headline: Team Lead Designer at übernatural · 400+ websites, 3 Awwwards
title: It will never be perfect. Stop.
text:
Every designer on my team wants one more pass on the hero.
So do I, after 400+ websites and 3 Awwwards.

Most designers suffer from perfectionism. There's always something you want to change, on every project, including the ones we send to Awwwards.

It will never be perfect.

You have to hand the work in on time and tell yourself: stop.

Our sites ship in about 72 hours. On that clock, one more pass on the hero is a missed deadline.

So before anything ships, a person answers two questions. Is the idea there? Is it actually beautiful?

If both answers are yes, we stop.

author: Egor Galiy
headline: Team Lead Designer at übernatural · 400+ websites, 3 Awwwards
title: Half of designers ship AI code
text:
Half of designers now say they've shipped AI-written code to a live product.
Most of them don't understand code.

That's from this year's AI in Design report: 900+ designers in 60+ countries. 91% use AI for design every week. A year earlier it was 54%.

To me this is more a question about code than about design. Designers use the code however the model spits it out, without much checking.

The first risk is legal. A form collects people's data, the designer has no idea about the laws, and they end up violating consumer rights without knowing it.

The second is security. If you don't know what's under the hood, your product is easier to hack.

In our studio, on projects that collect data, we build out all the legal pages and do everything by the law.

And we don't take projects with important databases. A serious one needs a whole separate person just for security, and that isn't the work we do.

If a fast, cheap site is about to collect your customers' data, ask who read the code.

author: Egor Galiy
headline: Team Lead Designer at übernatural · 400+ websites, 3 Awwwards
title: Taste by swipe
text:
Clients used to explain their taste to us on an hour-long call.
Now they get a link.

Behind the link is a set of 50 to 100 reference photos. One at a time, like it or skip it.

By the end we know how they want their site to look, and nobody had to find the words for it.

There's a clear goal there, and that thing really works. It saves about an hour per client.

We built a similar swiping tool for ourselves, to rate our own concepts.

That one is kind of a pointless exercise for now. It's unclear what criteria people use when they swipe, and what we care about is how a concept performs.

The client version stayed.

I once drafted a post about it called "Tinder plus Pinterest". Still the best description.

If you're planning a new site and want to try it, happy to send you the link.

author: Egor Galiy
headline: Team Lead Designer at übernatural · 400+ websites, 3 Awwwards
title: Framer: from a design studio to 188,000 companies
text:
Framer's founders ran a design studio before building the tool we ship every site on.
They sold that studio to Facebook in 2011, then Koen Bok and Jorn van Dijk built Framer.

This June, Framer said 188,000 companies in 200 countries build on it, 14x more than a year before. Over four million published sites, about 364 million visitors a month.

The same month it launched Framer Agents: AI that edits pages, components, CMS content and SEO inside the canvas.

We build in Framer every day, including with its AI. My honest split, from real builds:

Figma Make can do maybe 20% of a real website. It lays out blocks, but it can't make a nice looking design, and I have to clean up its layout.

Framer's AI works with Framer's actual features: animations, colour changes in the library, headers set up properly, decent responsiveness. I can hand it 25 to 30% of the work and go do something else.

My hypothesis is that AI should eventually do 60 to 70% of a fast website. We're building the habit now.

The idea and the look stay with a person. If you're weighing Framer for your next site, happy to chat.

author: Bogdan Chechin
headline: Co-founder at übernatural · Websites for founders and enterprises
title: Five months of shifting rectangles
text:
A lot of website projects are still quoted at five months

I always want to ask one question. What exactly happens during those five months? Shifting rectangles?

A website has a known list of parts. Structure, copy, visuals, the build, the fixes. None of them takes a month

The time goes into waiting. For a free slot in the studio's calendar, for the next weekly call, for the day the designer feels like creating

We cut the waiting. Our timeline is three days, and the only thing that sets it is one session a day with the client, because busy people can't review a website more often than that

I'm still curious what happens in week 7 of a five-month website. If you've been on the buying side of one, I'd like to hear it

author: Bogdan Chechin
headline: Co-founder at übernatural · Websites for founders and enterprises
title: The AI-made website bubble
text:
Many "AI made this website" posts show sites built by real design studios

Some of those sites won awards. The label says AI anyway

So people start believing a beautiful website is one prompt away. It still isn't easy to create a beautiful website. Everyone just shouts that it is

Founders try it, build something, and show it to each other. Everyone in the group agrees it looks great. To them, it does

Outside that group, a buyer sees a layout they have already seen many times this week and forms an opinion before reading a word

The people it hurts most are small freelancers doing real work, who now compete with a promise that was never true

The clients who come to us already know the difference. Not one of them ever came to us from AI

author: Bogdan Chechin
headline: Co-founder at übernatural · Websites for founders and enterprises
title: Faster means pay more
text:
If a client says we should charge less for working faster, I say: pay more

If you want to pay less, we can do it slower

Nothing else would change. Same people, same quality, same site. You would just wait longer for it

Speed is how a service business earns more with the same people. The client gets the site in 3 days, and there's room to pay the team more for the same hours

There's a second effect. Some clients come to us only for the speed. They already have an agency, it just can't ship by the date their launch needs

And a real chunk of clients tell us we could go slower. I ask what would change if we did. So far nobody has told me

If your launch date is fixed and your agency can't hit it, happy to chat

author: Bogdan Chechin
headline: Co-founder at übernatural · Websites for founders and enterprises
title: The comments prove it
text:
If you're still worried AI will replace you, scroll through the comments under any LinkedIn post

Pangram checked public LinkedIn posts from April to June 2026. About 30% of the comments were written entirely by AI

Everyone got the same model on the same day. A lot of people used it to write "Great insights, thanks for sharing" at scale

The tool only made the gap in effort easier to see

Every technical revolution goes the same way. The people who were going to do thoughtful work do more of it. Everyone else produces more of what they produced before

Average is what you get from the tools everyone has. So when a business needs something far from average, the input still has to come from people who care about the result

author: Bogdan Chechin
headline: Co-founder at übernatural · Websites for founders and enterprises
title: The client's calendar is the limit
text:
The fastest any service business can move is one client meeting a day

We learned it on websites. We once promised a site in a single day. The build fit into a day. The client's attention didn't

A founder or a head of marketing has a board, a product, a team, investors. To look at a website properly they need a clear hour, and most of them get one a day. More contact than that and the client starts working for the studio

So the real timeline is a count of sessions. Three sessions, three days, and we moved to three on purpose

Everything on our side is tuned to one target: get as much done as possible between two sessions. Quality stays fixed, speed is the variable

I suspect it holds for lawyers, consultants and builders too. Worth checking whose calendar sets the pace in your own business. In ours it's the client's

author: Bogdan Chechin
headline: Co-founder at übernatural · Websites for founders and enterprises
title: Dubai: 71% of deals were off-plan
text:
71% of Dubai's property deals this year were for buildings that don't exist yet

In the first half of 2026 the city recorded 87,800 real estate deals worth AED 291.7 billion. Seven in ten were off-plan (MERED, H1 2026 report)

So most buyers here pay for a promise. A view nobody can stand in yet

Until the tower is finished, the buyer has a render, a brochure and a website. For two or three years, that is the product

Which changes the math on the website. On a nine-figure tower it's a rounding error in the budget. It's also the thing every buyer, broker and bank opens first, often from another continent

I'd file it under sales, next to the show apartment

One of our clients owns skyscrapers in New York. What I took from that work: the site's real job is to make a room that doesn't exist yet feel real

author: Bogdan Chechin
headline: Co-founder at übernatural · Websites for founders and enterprises
title: You can't sue a prompt
text:
You can't sue a prompt. In May, a German court made that official

A clinic's website chatbot invented specialist titles for its doctors, qualifications that the medical rules don't recognise

The Higher Regional Court of Hamm held the clinic responsible. A chatbot that acts on behalf of a company is not a third party. What it says is the company's statement, however carefully it was configured

In August a US appeals court got there from another direction. In Amazon v. Perplexity, the Ninth Circuit called an AI agent "a tool, not a person"

That's my main argument for why companies will keep paying people and firms even when models do most of the work. Someone has to answer for the result, and a model can't

AI agents can already hold a bank card. Nobody has built them a way to carry a loss. My hunch is that one day a protocol will pool part of every agent's fees to cover exactly that. Until then, the liability sits with a human who has a name and a contract

For anyone buying a website, it's a boring point that matters. A fixed price, a fixed date, and someone who answers for both

author: Bogdan Chechin
headline: Co-founder at übernatural · Websites for founders and enterprises
title: Lovable and the price of average
text:
Lovable is worth $13.3 billion. Its revenue run rate just passed $600 million

A million new projects a week. Two thirds of the Fortune 500 have users on it

In our market it's the clearest example of basic supply and demand. When the supply of something becomes almost infinite, its price falls toward zero. Anyone can now get a decent-looking website for the price of a subscription

We felt it directly. Most of the small clients who used to write to us now build it themselves

The bigger ones stayed, from funded startups to Dubai Fintech District. For a startup that raised $3M, a company selling towers or a team pitching a ministry, the website has one job: to look unlike the million built this week, before the first call

So the market split in two. Self-service at one end. At the other, people who want something far from average and would rather pay someone who does it well

Lovable is a great business. It's also the best argument I know for why outstanding design gets more expensive from here

If you've raised and your site looks like this week's million, happy to chat

title: Things buyers hear from agencies

Things buyers hear before they ever see their website

author: Bogdan Chechin
headline: Co-founder at übernatural · Websites for founders and enterprises
title: One hour, 1,000,000 users
text:
At 19 I built a Telegram bot in about an hour. Then we forgot about it for almost 3 years

A birthday bot. No marketing, no plan, no updates

When we finally opened the stats it had 110,000 users. All organic. We were properly stunned

We rebuilt it. It passed 1,000,000 users, growing by 10,000 to 20,000 a day, and the birthday "gift" broadcasts converted at about 2%
